title: Quant fallout field lab: kernel-specific quality vs latency mapping
body:
Purpose:
This is a field-lab style writeup of a short, targeted investigation into quantization-induced performance and quality fallout that only appears on a small subset of request shapes and kernels. Goal: produce a reproducible mapping from workload fingerprint -> (kernel, quantization) -> observed quality delta and latency tail regression, and propose lightweight mitigations for production routing/fallbacks.

Background / motivation:
- We've shipped several quant kernels (AWQ, GPTQ variants, int8 packed kernels, and fp8 experimental paths). Overall throughput/latency wins are real, but ops have reported intermittent customer incidents where high-quality prompts degrade unexpectedly after a rollout. Those incidents tend to show: stable median latency but large p99 jumps and small but measurable quality regressions on particular prompts (long context, many rare tokens, or heavy prefix reuse).
- Hypothesis: subtle numerical noise patterns plus kernel micro-behavior (tiling, lane branching) interact with key routing/caching heuristics and cause two distinct failure modes: (A) latency amplification via kernel thrashing / cache invalidation, and (B) small quality drop concentrated in specific token spans due to per-layer quant rounding artifacts.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Models: open-7B-v2 (decoder), redwood-chat-2B (small convo sim), llama2-13B-like trimmed (for tiling stress)
- Quant modes: AWQ-3bit (baseline field), GPTQ-4bit, INT8 symmetric, FP8-e4m3 experimental
- Kernels: vector-lane-packed, tile-128, tile-256, dispatch-multiplex (mixed lane), fallback-slow (reference fp16 path)
- Workload shapes: short chat (<=128 tokens), long-context narrative (4096 and 8192 prefixes), high-repeat-token prefix (heavy KV reuse), adversarial token distribution (rare unicode + punctuation)
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 16 (to trigger multiplexing paths)
- Hardware: A100-SXM-80GB (driver 525.85), H100-PCI-80GB (driver 535.54), M60 (simulated lower bandwidth)
- Measurement window: 6h continuous replay per combination, synthetic traffic plus 10k sampled customer prompts that previously tripped incidents.

Methodology / metrics collected:
- Latency: p50, p95, p99, p999 token-step latency, cold-start first-token latency
- Throughput: tokens/sec, useful-tokens/sec (excludes padding)
- Quality: token-level logprob drift vs fp16 reference, perplexity delta, top-k token distribution shift, and a small human-rated quality score on 500 samples (A/B blind comparing quant vs fp16 for flagged failures)
- System: GPU util, DRAM bandwidth, kernel occupancy, dispatcher queue depth, cache eviction events (KV cache misses), and kernel preemption counts
- Logging: per-token debug traces captured for failing flows (limited sample to avoid storage explosion)

Key results (high-level summaries):
- Latency fallout archetype A (thrash): On AWQ + dispatch-multiplex kernel with long-context 8192+ prefixes and batch >=4, we observed p99 token-step latency increase of 2.1x compared to the same config on tile-128 packing. The root cause appears to be uneven kernel occupancy leading to repeated small preemptions and dispatcher retries.
- Quality fallout archetype B (drift): On GPTQ-4bit with vector-lane-packed kernel and adversarial token distribution, we saw a median token logprob drift of ~0.25 nats and a small but systematic top-1 token shift for certain punctuation and rare unicode tokens. Human blind rating on the 500-sample set showed a mean drop of 0.28 points (on a 5-point scale) vs fp16.
- INT8 symmetric performed well on throughput but showed a narrow class of failure: when sequence length included many short contiguous repeated tokens (e.g., markdown-heavy prefixes), quantized accumulators in tile-256 path saturate and produce occasional token hallucinations (rare, ~0.03% of tokens).
- FP8 path delivered best fidelity (negligible perplexity delta) but at cost of ~10-12% higher median latency on H100 due to extra format conversion costs in our runtime (opportunity to fuse).

Representative numeric snapshots:
- open-7B-v2, AWQ + dispatch-multiplex, long context 8192, batch=4 on A100:
  - p50 token-step: 6.8ms (vs fp16 6.5ms)
  - p99 token-step: 58ms (vs fp16 27ms)
  - kernel preemptions per request: 14 (vs fp16 2)
  - human quality delta: -0.02 (not significant)

- llama-like 13B, GPTQ-4bit + vector-lane-packed, adversarial tokens, batch=1 on H100:
  - perplexity delta: +3.1% relative to fp16
  - mean token logprob drift: 0.25 nats
  - blind human rating delta: -0.28 /5
  - p99 latency: 34ms (vs fp16 28ms)

Findings and interpretation:
1) Two distinct mechanisms drive "fallout": scheduling/occupancy-driven latency amplification (mostly triggered by multiplexed/dispatch kernels under long-context + batching) and numerical/artifact-driven quality drift (mostly in very low-bit GPTQ/AWQ packing on vector-lane codegen).
2) The incidents that hit customers historically align better with the latency amplification archetype — those look like traffic shape regressions rather than pure quantization fidelity issues.
3) Kernel micro-choices matter: tile size, lane packing, and whether the kernel supports atomic KV-prefetch interaction strongly influence eviction patterns. Some kernels expose nondeterministic ordering that amplifies dispatcher queue jitter.
4) FP8 buys fidelity at modest perf cost; in tight SLO workloads it can be a useful fallback for safety-critical routes.

Lightweight mitigations tested (quick wins):
- Profile-guided routing rule: sample 1% of traffic per route and run a micro-fingerprint (seq len distribution, repeat-token ratio, rare-token score). If fingerprint matches high-risk bucket, route to fp16/fp8 or to tile-128 kernel. Implemented as routing rule prototype and tested on synthetic: reduced p99 regressions by 70% for the flagged traffic at ~0.5% overall extra cost.
- Per-layer fallback toggles: allow per-request override to use fp16 for a small set of attention layers (top-2 layers) where drift concentrated. This hybrid cut reduced perplexity delta by 60% while incurring only 8% latency overhead vs full fp16 for the same request shapes.
- Kernel backoff: when dispatcher preemption counts exceed threshold, force immediate fallback to a non-multiplex kernel to avoid prolonged thrash. This avoids the 2x p99 spike in most reproductions.

Action items / next steps:
- Short term (1–2 sprints): land the profile-guided routing prototype behind a flag, build telemetry to map live traffic into our fingerprint buckets, and add a Canary to automatic fallbacks (SERV-1873).
- Mid term (3–6 months): implement a fused FP8 conversion path in the runtime kernels to reduce the FP8 overhead and reassess cost/fidelity tradeoffs.
- Research: run a systematic per-layer sensitivity scan (staggered per-layer quant toggles) across model families to create a small rulebook for hybrid layer-level fallbacks.
- Ops: add an alert that correlates rising kernel preemption counts + p99 tail increase so SREs can triage earlier.

Open questions / unresolved:
- How stable are these token-level drift signatures across model versions (we tested 7B/13B variants but need more model families).
- Can the dispatcher be modified to provide stronger ordering guarantees without losing throughput? That would reduce thrash but is nontrivial.
- Are there specific micro-ops or instruction sequences (particularly on H100) that amplify FP8 conversion cost spikes under our current CUDA schedule? Need kernel-level profiling with NVIDIA tools.

Repro steps (short):
1) Checkout PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime@bench/quant-fallout (linked above).
2) Launch bench harness with replay set: artifacts/replay/quant-fallout-10k.tar.gz (sensitive; request via ops).
3) Run matrix command (example): ./bench/run.sh --model open-7B-v2 --kernel dispatch-multiplex --quant awq --seq 8192 --batch 4 --duration 6h --trace-sample 200
4) Collect traces from /mnt/bench/output/<run>/ and run python tools/quant_analysis.py --summarize to produce p99 vs kernel preemption plots.

Notes to self / informal observations:
- The human blind score drop was small but consistent across annotators; worth further lightweight eval before we panic.
- We should add a small "stress fingerprint" test to our CI that combines repeat-token-heavy prefix + long context at small batch to catch regressions earlier.

Appendix (raw logs pointers and quick charts):
- sample trace excerpt: /mnt/bench/output/run-2029-09-18/trace-4321.txt
- p99-vs-preempt csv: /mnt/bench/output/run-2029-09-18/p99_preempt.csv
- quick flamegraph (AWQ dispatch-multiplex): /mnt/bench/output/run-2029-09-18/flame-awq-dispatch.svg

If this looks reasonable I'll spin up a lightweight canary and get product/ops alignment for rolling to the risky routes (goal: reduce customer-facing incidents with minimal cost impact).

— Aisha K.
